course: Course 4: Operating Systems and Embedded Linux
audience: Anyone who can write a little C (Course 3, Chapters 0 to 10, is enough to start), through college students and working embedded engineers.
approach: Every idea is shown running on a real Linux system on your own laptop: commands you type, C programs you compile, and from Part 7 a complete ARM Linux system booted in QEMU, the emulator. A Raspberry Pi is optional; every lab has a laptop version. Every command and program on every page is run by our test suite before publication, and its output is checked.
tested_on: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on x86-64, gcc 13.3, QEMU 8.2 (user mode and system mode), aarch64-linux-gnu cross toolchain.

tiers.E1: First steps: check the idea with short, direct exercises
tiers.E2: University exams: operating systems and embedded systems courses
tiers.E3: Interviews: embedded, firmware and systems engineering interviews
tiers.E4: Labs and projects: build, measure and debug on Linux, QEMU and a Raspberry Pi
tiers.E5: Kernel and professional: kernel source, real drivers and production practice

depth_standard: Every idea is shown running: a command, a C program or a QEMU lab, with its real output.
Every chapter goes underneath: what the kernel, the C library and the hardware actually do, on x86 and on ARM.
Every lab works on a laptop. Where real hardware adds something, a Raspberry Pi version is given as an option.
A problem ladder with full solutions climbs through the tiers the topic supports.
Quantum connections appear only where they are real: the controllers of today's quantum computers are FPGA boards running embedded Linux.
